notes.ACC: The accounting and financial reporting ecosystem exists because outsiders supply capital to firms they do not manage. It converts private economic activity into trusted, comparable public information.

notes.IASB: The International Accounting Standards Board sets IFRS. It is influential worldwide but has no sovereign authority — standards only become compulsory when a national legislature adopts or endorses them.
notes.MASB: The Malaysian Accounting Standards Board, created by the Financial Reporting Act 1997, issues the MFRS Framework (word-for-word IFRS-equivalent) and MPERS for eligible private entities.
notes.FS: Financial statements are the central artifact of the whole system: produced by the entity, audited by assurance, filed with regulators, and read by every user group.

notes.C: The 'reporting constitution' is the conceptual foundation every later system obeys: objectives, rules, element definitions, and recognition/measurement principles.
notes.ATB: The adjusted trial balance is the checkpoint between raw bookkeeping and the financial statements — every adjustment in System 3 lands here.

notes.CH1: Introduces the two core statements, the entity types (sole trader, partnership, limited liability company), the full list of users from management to shareholders, and corporate governance as the system by which entities are directed and controlled.
notes.CH2: The IFRS Foundation appoints and oversees the IASB (IFRS Standards), the ISSB (sustainability disclosures), the Advisory Council (agenda advice) and IFRIC (interpretations where no standard exists).
notes.CH3: The Conceptual Framework: accrual accounting and going concern underpin the objective; relevance and faithful representation are fundamental; comparability, verifiability, timeliness and understandability enhance; benefits must justify cost. Defines the five elements and the historical-cost versus current-value measurement bases.
notes.CH3E: Historical cost is most common: measured at transaction date, not updated. Current value includes fair value, value in use / fulfilment value, and current cost.

notes.CH4: Documents flow from quotation through orders, goods received/despatched notes, invoices, credit/debit notes, remittance advice and receipt. Sales and purchase invoices and credit notes are what enter the accounting records. Computerised systems centre on the general ledger with receivables, payables, non-current asset and inventory modules.
notes.CH5: Every statement line has a ledger account, often drawn as a T account. Total debits must equal total credits: a debit increases assets, expenses and drawings (DEAD); a credit increases liabilities, income and capital (CLIC).
notes.CH6: Balancing off every account produces the trial balance, from which the statement of profit or loss (period performance) and statement of financial position (point-in-time snapshot) are drawn. Assets = capital + liabilities throughout.

notes.CH7: Inventory is measured at the lower of cost (FIFO or AVCO, including costs to bring it to present location and condition) and net realisable value (sales price less costs to complete and sell). In rising prices FIFO gives higher closing inventory and higher profit.
notes.CH8: Capital expenditure creates a non-current asset at cost (purchase price plus directly attributable costs); repairs are expenses. Depreciate straight-line (even use) or diminishing-balance (front-loaded benefits); land is not depreciated. Revaluation is a policy choice applied to a whole class. On disposal, proceeds versus carrying amount gives profit or loss.
notes.CH9: Research expenditure is written off as incurred. Development expenditure must be capitalised when the PIRATE criteria are all satisfied, then amortised over its finite life.
notes.CH10: Accruals: expenses incurred but unpaid (liability); prepayments: paid in advance (asset). Mirror rules for accrued income (asset) and deferred income (liability).
notes.CH11: Recognise a provision only when there is a present obligation, a probable transfer of economic benefit, and a reliable estimate. Contingent liabilities and (probable) contingent assets are disclosed in the notes, not recognised.
notes.CH12: Irrecoverable debts are written off to expense. An allowance covers specific doubtful debts plus a percentage of the rest; only the movement in the allowance hits profit or loss.
notes.CH13: Output tax is charged on sales, input tax paid on purchases; the difference is settled with the tax authority. Irrecoverable sales tax is included in the cost of the purchase.
notes.CH14: Trade receivables/payables in the general ledger are control totals; individual customer and supplier balances live in separate ledgers outside the double-entry system. Supplier statements are reconciled against the payables ledger.

notes.CH15: A credit balance on the bank statement means money in the bank; a debit balance means overdrawn. Differences are timing (outstanding lodgements, unpresented cheques) or business errors (omissions, transpositions, casting).
notes.CH16: Errors of omission, commission, principle, compensating and transposition may or may not break the trial balance; a suspense account holds the difference until each error is identified and corrected. Corrections can change reported profit.
notes.CH17: With incomplete records, reconstruct figures using cost structures (margin = gross profit % of sales; mark-up = % of cost), T-account workings for credit sales and purchases, drawings, and the accounting equation: assets = liabilities + capital + profit − drawings.

notes.CH18: Technique chapter: work from the trial balance through the key adjustments — closing inventory, drawings, depreciation, irrecoverable debts, accruals and prepayments, receivables and payables — to complete statements.
notes.CH19: Company finance: issues at a premium (excess credited to share premium), rights issues (below market, to existing holders), bonus issues (free, funded from reserves); reserves; long-term borrowings with interest to profit or loss; income tax as a current liability; dividends as appropriations of retained earnings.
notes.CH20: Full company statements: SPLOCI (realised gains in profit or loss, unrealised in OCI), SoFP, statement of changes in equity, and examinable disclosure notes. IFRS 15: recognise revenue when control of goods or services transfers to the customer.
notes.CH21: Events between the reporting date and authorisation of the statements: adjusting events evidence conditions that existed at the reporting date (court case resolution, customer bankruptcy); non-adjusting events arose after it (fire, share transactions, proposed dividends) and are disclosed if material.
notes.CH22: IAS 7 groups cash movements into operating (indirect method adjusts operating profit for non-cash items and working capital; direct method uses gross receipts and payments), investing and financing activities.
notes.CH23: Three investment types: subsidiary (control — consolidate), associate (significant influence — equity account), trade investment (neither). Group statements present the parent and subsidiaries as a single entity.
notes.CH24: Consolidated SoFP: goodwill = consideration + NCI − fair value of net assets acquired; add 100% of subsidiary assets and liabilities; eliminate the parent's investment, inter-company balances and unrealised profit; pro-rate for mid-year acquisitions.
notes.CH25: Consolidated SoPL: cancel intra-group revenue and cost of sales, remove unrealised profit on inventory still held, and pro-rate the subsidiary's results and NCI for mid-year acquisitions.

notes.CH26: Ratio families: profitability (gross and operating margin, ROCE, ROE), liquidity (current, quick), efficiency (inventory turnover, receivables collection, payables payment, working capital cycle, asset turnover), position (interest cover, gearing). Note obvious trends before calculating, and mind the limitations.
notes.CH26F: Ratios mislead under inflation, differing accounting policies, seasonal trading, unrepresentative year-ends, related party transactions, differing ratio definitions, manipulated statements, or a new company with no comparatives.

notes.FSB: Statement of profit or loss: a record of revenue (income) generated and expenditure incurred over a given period. Revenue is the income generated by the operations of the business for the period; expenses are the costs of running the business for the same period. Statement of financial position: simply a list of all the assets owned and all the liabilities owed by the business as at a particular date.
notes.FS3: An asset is a present economic resource controlled by the entity as a result of past events. An economic resource is a right that has the potential to produce economic benefits.
notes.FS4: A liability is a present obligation of the entity to transfer economic resource as a result of past events. An obligation is a duty of responsibility that the entity has no practical ability to avoid.
notes.FS5: Equity is the residual interest in the assets of the entity after deducting all its liabilities.
notes.ENT: Sole trader: a sole tradership is a business owned and run by one individual. Partnership: arrangements between individuals to carry on business in common with a view to profit. Limited liability company: limited liability status means that the business's debts and the personal debts of the business's owners (shareholders) are legally separate.
notes.USR: The users of financial statements: management, government, public, lenders, analysts and advisers, third parties, employees, shareholders.
notes.CG: Corporate governance is the system by which companies and other entities are directed and controlled.

notes.IFRSF: Appoints members to the IASB, IFRIC and IFRS Advisory Council, oversees the regulatory system and raises the finance to support it.
notes.AC: Advises the IASB on its agenda and timetable for developing IFRS Standards, and advises the IASB of areas that may need to be considered by the IFRIC.
notes.IASB: Issues IFRS Standards and revised IASs. It is an independent standard setter made up of representatives from different global economies.
notes.ISSB: Delivers sustainability-related disclosure standards that provide investors with information about companies' sustainability-related risks and opportunities to help them make informed decisions.
notes.IFRIC: Issues guidance on how to apply existing IFRS Standards and how to account for new financial reporting issues where no IFRS Standard exists. It reports to the IASB.
notes.STD: IFRS Standards provide guidance as to how transactions and events should be recognised, measured, presented and disclosed in financial statements.

ch3.title: Ch 3 — Qualitative Characteristics of Financial Information

notes.OBJ: Accrual accounting: the effects of transactions and other events are recognised when they occur, even if the resultant cash receipts or payments occur in a different period. Going concern: the financial statements are normally prepared on the assumption that the entity is a going concern and will continue in operation for the foreseeable future.
notes.FU1: Relevance: capable of making a difference in the decisions made by users — predictive and/or confirmatory value; materiality.
notes.FU2: Faithful representation: represents economic phenomena in words and numbers, reflects substance, complete, neutral, free from error.
notes.ENH: Comparability: about other entities and other periods. Verifiability: information must be capable of being verified. Timeliness: information must be available in time to influence decision making. Understandability: information must be classified and presented in a clear and concise manner.
notes.COST: The benefits of reporting financial information must justify the costs incurred to provide and use it.
notes.ELEM: Asset: present economic resource controlled by the entity as a result of past events. Liability: a present obligation of an entity to transfer an economic resource as a result of past events. Equity: the residual interest in the assets after deducting all liabilities. Income: increases in assets or decreases in liabilities that result in increases in equity, other than those relating to contributions from holders of equity claims. Expenses: decreases in assets or increases in liabilities that result in decreases in equity, other than those relating to distributions to holders of equity claims.
notes.MEAS: Historical cost: most common; measured at the transaction date and not subsequently updated — asset: cost of acquisition/creation plus transaction costs; liability: value to incur/take on less transaction costs. Current value: updated to reflect changes in value at the measurement date — fair value (price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants), value in use for assets / fulfilment value for liabilities (present value of the cash flows expected from the asset, or expected to be obliged to transfer to fulfil the liability), and current cost (cost of an equivalent asset or consideration for an equivalent liability at the measurement date).

ch4.title: Ch 4 — Financial Transactions and Accounting Systems

notes.DOC: The documents: quotation, purchase order, sales order, goods received note, goods despatched note, sales invoice and supplier (purchase) invoice, supplier statement, credit note, debit note, remittance advice, receipt.
notes.REC: The documents that enter the accounting records include: sales invoices, sales credit notes, purchase invoices and purchase credit notes.
notes.SYS: Accounting software: off-the-shelf or bespoke package. The main accounting module is the 'general ledger'; other accounting modules include the receivables ledger, payables ledger, non-current assets register and inventory system. Key features of computerised accounting systems: controls, standing data and account codes. Access: software installed on local computers or cloud-based accounting software.

ch5.title: Ch 5 — Ledger Accounts and Double Entry

notes.LED: Each item in the statement of financial position or statement of profit or loss will have an 'account'. Ledger accounts are often shown as 'T' accounts. At the end of the year/period, each ledger account is balanced off and the totals taken to the trial balance.
notes.DE: TOTAL DEBITS = TOTAL CREDITS. A debit entry increases assets, expenses and drawings, and a credit entry increases liabilities, income and capital — this can be remembered as DEAD CLIC.

ch6.title: Ch 6 — From Trial Balance to Financial Statements

notes.TB1: A list of all the assets, liabilities, capital, income and expenses of a business in debit and credit columns.
notes.PL: Shows all the income and expenses of a business over a period of time.
notes.FP: Shows all the assets and liabilities of a business at a point in time — a 'snapshot' of the position of the business.

notes.VAL: Cost: cost of purchase, cost of conversion, and other costs incurred in bringing the inventory to its present location and condition. Two methods of estimating cost: FIFO (first in first out) and AVCO (average cost). Net realisable value: sales price, less costs to complete, less selling and distribution costs. Effect on profit and assets: in times of rising prices, FIFO produces a higher closing inventory figure, a lower cost of sales figure and therefore a higher profit figure than AVCO.
notes.ADJ: Opening inventory: Dr Opening inventory (SPL), Cr Inventory (SOFP). Closing inventory: Dr Inventory (SOFP), Cr Closing inventory (SPL).

notes.EXP: Asset expenditure results in a non-current asset being shown on the statement of financial position. Other expenditure, such as repairs and maintenance, is shown as an expense in the statement of profit or loss.
notes.CST: Tangible non-current assets should initially be recorded at cost: the purchase price of the item plus any directly attributable costs to bring the item to its intended location and ready to use.
notes.DEP: Depreciation is an expense charged in relation to the asset each year to reflect the using up of the asset; land usually has an unlimited useful life and so is not depreciated. Straight line: suitable for assets which are used up evenly during their lifetime — the depreciation expense is the same each year. Diminishing balance: suitable where the benefits obtained by the business from using the asset decline over time — the depreciation expense is higher in the initial years. Accounting: Dr Depreciation expense (SPL), Cr Accumulated depreciation (SOFP).
notes.REV: An entity may choose to revalue its assets rather than hold them at cost — this is a choice of accounting policy. Where an entity revalues, it must revalue all assets in the same class, and the depreciation charge is based on the revalued amount.
notes.DIS: On disposal, the sales proceeds are compared to the carrying amount of the asset to calculate the profit or loss on disposal. Where an asset is given in part exchange for another asset, the part-exchange allowance takes the place of the sales proceeds. Entries: Dr Disposal account, Cr Cost of asset account; Dr Accumulated depreciation, Cr Disposal account; Dr Cash account, Cr Disposal account. The balancing figure in the disposals account is the profit or loss on disposal.

notes.RES: Research: no guarantee that the expenditure will generate profit — write the expenditure off in the year it is incurred. Accounting treatment: show as an expense in the SOPL — Dr Research expenditure, Cr Bank.
notes.DEV: Development: future profits are expected — must capitalise as an intangible non-current asset if all of the relevant criteria of PIRATE are satisfied. Accounting treatment: capitalise on the SOFP — Dr Intangible non-current asset, Cr Bank/payables.
notes.AMO: If the intangible asset has a finite life, amortise over that life: Dr Amortisation expense, Cr Intangible non-current asset.

notes.DEF: Accruals: income or expenses that have occurred during the period but are unpaid at the year end. Prepayments: income or expenses that are paid for in advance of the period they relate to.
notes.ACC: Although unpaid: accrued expenses are included in expenses for the period and are a liability at the year end — Dr Expenses (SPL), Cr Accrued expenses (SOFP). Accrued income is included in income for the period and is an asset at the year end — Dr Accrued income (SOFP), Cr Income (SPL).
notes.PRE: Although paid in advance: prepaid expenses are not included in expenses in the period they are paid and are an asset at the year end — Dr Prepaid expenses (SOFP), Cr Expenses (SPL). Deferred (prepaid) income is not included as income in the period the money is received and is a liability at the year end — Dr Income (SPL), Cr Deferred income (SOFP).

notes.PRO: Provision: a liability of uncertain timing or amount. Recognition criteria: present obligation, probable transfer of economic benefit, reliable estimate. Accounting treatment: increase in provision — Dr Expense (SPL), Cr Provision (SOFP); decrease in provision — Dr Provision (SOFP), Cr Expense (SPL).
notes.CL: A possible obligation, or a present obligation that is not recognised because it is not probable that there will be a transfer of economic benefit or the amount cannot be measured reliably. Disclose in the notes.
notes.CA: A possible asset that arises from past events and whose existence will be confirmed only by the occurrence or non-occurrence of one or more uncertain future events not wholly within the control of the entity. Disclose in the notes.

notes.IRR: Irrecoverable debts: debts which the company believes the customer will never pay. Accounting treatment: they are written off to the irrecoverable debts expense account — Dr Irrecoverable debts account (SPL), Cr Receivables. Debts written off subsequently recovered: if the customer then pays the outstanding amount, the expense needs to be reversed — Dr Cash at bank (SOFP), Cr Irrecoverable debts account (SPL).
notes.ALL: Businesses may make an allowance for a specific debt that they might not recover, and also take a percentage of outstanding receivables as a prudent precaution for the possibility that some other customers may not pay. Create: Dr Irrecoverable debts expense (SPL), Cr Allowance for irrecoverable debts (SOFP). Adjusting: increase the allowance — Dr Irrecoverable debts expense (SPL), Cr Allowance (SOFP); decrease the allowance — Dr Allowance (SOFP), Cr Irrecoverable debts expense (SPL).

notes.OUT: Output tax is charged on sales. Accounting treatment: Dr Trade receivables SOFP (gross amount), Cr Sales SPL (net amount), Cr Sales tax account (SOFP).
notes.INP: Input tax is paid on purchases. Accounting treatment: Dr Purchases SPL (net amount), Dr Sales tax account (SOFP), Cr Trade payables SOFP (gross amount).
notes.IRRT: Irrecoverable sales tax must be included in the cost of the purchase.
notes.RATE: The rates of sales tax are decided by the tax authorities in the relevant country and these rates will be provided in the exam.

ch14.title: Ch 14 — Trade Receivables and Trade Payables

notes.TER: In the general ledger: trade receivables is the total owed by all credit customers; trade payables is the total owed to all credit suppliers. Receivables and payables ledgers (outside the general ledger): the receivables ledger holds the balance owed by each individual credit customer; the payables ledger the balance owed to each individual credit supplier.
notes.OTH: Contra entries always reduce the outstanding balance. Returns, credit notes, refunds and overpayments: return of goods cancels the original purchase/sale — on return of goods a payables balance will show a debit and a receivables balance a credit; refund of payment returns the balance to zero. Discounts: trade discounts are given at the time of purchase, always taken up, and the transaction is recorded net of discount; settlement discounts are offered as encouragement to settle the bill early, are not always taken up, and the transaction is recorded net of discount only if the discount is expected to be taken up.
notes.SUP: Supplier statements should be compared to the payables ledger to identify and correct any errors. The supplier's statement and the payables ledger do not form part of the double-entry system.

notes.REC: Compare the bank general ledger account balance with the bank statement balance. On the statement: a credit balance means money in the bank; a debit balance means the account is overdrawn.
notes.TIM: Timing differences: outstanding lodgements — deposits credited after date; unpresented or outstanding cheques.
notes.ERR: Errors by the business: omissions, transposition errors, casting errors.

notes.TYP: Types of error: omission, commission, principle, compensating, transposition, unequal double entry.
notes.SUS: The suspense account is a temporary account. Purpose: temporary posting of entries when uncertain of the correct accounting, or to make the trial balance balance. To clear a suspense account: identify the original incorrect entry, identify the correction needed, make the adjustment.
notes.ADJ: Correction of errors can alter profits.

notes.CST: Cost of sales = opening inventories + purchases − closing inventories. Margin: gross profit expressed as a percentage of sales. Mark-up: gross profit expressed as a percentage of cost of sales.
notes.DER: Credit sales and receivables: use the information given in the scenario (opening and closing receivables, and sales) to derive missing figures such as money received from credit customers — remember to exclude cash sales from the T-account working. Credit purchases and payables: use opening and closing payables and purchases to derive missing figures such as payments to credit suppliers — exclude cash purchases. Drawings: owners of the business take goods or cash for their own use; where goods are withdrawn they are recorded at cost to the business. Inventory: use opening and closing inventory and purchases to derive missing figures.
notes.AEQ: Assets = liabilities + capital + profit − drawings. Rearrange to find a missing figure such as profit or drawings.

notes.ADJ: Key adjustments: closing inventory, drawings, depreciation, irrecoverable debts, accruals and prepayments, trade receivables and trade payables.

notes.SHA: Issue at a premium: when shares are issued at a premium to their nominal value, the excess is credited to the share premium account — Dr Cash, Cr Share capital, Cr Share premium. Rights issue: shares issued to existing shareholders at a rights price below the current market price; advantages — a cost-effective way for the company to raise finance, and if all rights are taken up shareholders maintain their percentage shareholding; disadvantages — 'bad press' for the company if all rights are not taken up, and an effect on future dividend policy. Bonus issue: shares issued for no cash consideration, always done at nominal value — Dr Reserves (SPA), Cr Share capital; advantages — enables the company to use the share premium account, and the falling share price makes shares more affordable to new investors; disadvantage — the rationale is not always understood by shareholders.
notes.RES: Reserves: share premium account, revaluation surplus, other reserves, retained earnings.
notes.FIN: Long-term borrowings: an alternative to raising finance by issuing shares; interest expenses will be incurred and charged to profit or loss. Income taxes: companies pay tax on profits earnt — an expense in profit or loss and a current liability in the statement of financial position.
notes.DIV: Dividends are appropriations of retained earnings to shareholders. Dividends on ordinary shares and irredeemable preference shares are debited to retained earnings. Dividends relating to redeemable preference shares are an interest expense in the statement of profit or loss.
notes.CMP: Sole trader: less regulation, owner personally liable for the debts of the business. Company: tighter regulation, owners separate from managers, liability limited to investment.

ch20.title: Ch 20 — Preparation of Financial Statements for Companies

notes.SPL: Shows the income and expenses for a period under specific headings. Points to note: SPL relates to realised gains and losses; OCI relates to unrealised gains and losses (posted directly to reserves). Distribution costs: delivery costs. Administrative expenses: general costs that do not 'fit' under the other captions. Interest expenses: bank interest, debenture and loan-note interest. Income tax expense: estimate of income tax due on the profits for the period plus or minus any under or over provision in respect of prior periods.
notes.FP: Shows the assets and liabilities of a business at a point in time.
notes.CE: Explains the movements between the equity section of the statement of financial position at the beginning and the end of the year. Key components: issue of share capital, dividends (on ordinary shares), total comprehensive income for the year, revaluation surplus on non-current assets, transfer to retained earnings.
notes.NT: Examinable notes: property plant and equipment, intangible non-current assets, inventory, provisions, contingent liabilities, contingent assets, events after the reporting period.
notes.IFRS15: Under IFRS 15 an entity recognises revenue to depict the transfer of goods or services to customers. Revenue is recognised when there is a transfer of control to the customer from the entity supplying the goods or services.

ch21.title: Ch 21 — Events After the Reporting Period

notes.DEF: Events, both favourable and unfavourable, that occur between the end of the reporting period and the date when the financial statements are authorised for issue.
notes.ADJ: Adjusting events provide evidence of conditions which existed at the end of the reporting period; include them in the financial statements. Examples: resolution of a court case, bankruptcy of a major customer, evidence of the NRV of inventories, discovery of fraud or errors.
notes.NON: Non-adjusting events relate to conditions which arose after the end of the reporting period; disclose in a note to the financial statements if material. Examples: destruction of a major asset by flood or fire, major share transactions, announcement of a plan to close part of a business, dividends proposed or declared after the end of the reporting period.

notes.IAS7: IAS 7 requires a company to show the movement in cash and cash equivalents between the beginning and the end of the year under three headings: cash flows from operating activities, investing activities, and financing activities.
notes.CE: Cash: cash on hand and demand deposits. Cash equivalents: short-term, highly liquid investments — for example current asset investments.
notes.OPR: Indirect method: cash generated from operations — adjust the operating profit figure for non-cash items, items shown elsewhere in the cash flow, and movements in working capital; then deduct interest and income taxes paid. Direct method: cash generated from operations derived by calculating cash receipts from customers and cash payments to suppliers and employees; then deduct interest and income taxes paid.
notes.INV: Cash flows relating to the acquisition or disposal of non-current assets and the returns on investments. Includes: purchase of non-current assets, proceeds from sale of non-current assets, interest and dividends received.
notes.FIN: Cash flows relating to the issue or repayment of long-term finance. Includes: proceeds from share capital or debenture issues, repayment of loans, ordinary dividends paid.

ch23.title: Ch 23 — Introduction to Consolidated Financial Statements

notes.TYP: Three types of investment (in the syllabus): subsidiary (control), associate (significant influence), trade investment (no influence).
notes.PAR: Parent's separate financial statements: SOFP — investment at cost (for the exam); SPLOCI — investment income, i.e. dividends.
notes.GRP: Consolidated accounts are prepared for a group of companies, for the parent's shareholders, in addition to the parent's individual financial statements, to show the group as a single business entity.
notes.CFP: Consolidated statement of financial position: add the parent plus 100% of the subsidiary's assets and liabilities line by line; cancel the investment with the subsidiary's share capital and pre-acquisition reserves; share capital/premium = parent only; reserves = parent plus group share of subsidiary post-acquisition.
notes.ASS: Accounting for associates — equity accounting: consolidated SOFP shows investment in associate (cost of associate plus share of post-acquisition reserves less impairment); consolidated SPLOCI shows the group percentage of the associate's profit for the year and percentage of the associate's OCI.

ch24.title: Ch 24 — Consolidated Statement of Financial Position

notes.GW: Goodwill: fair value of consideration plus fair value of NCI less fair value of net assets acquired (share capital, retained earnings and fair value adjustment at acquisition). Positive goodwill: capitalise as an intangible non-current asset. Negative goodwill: to the SPL.
notes.NCI: Non-controlling interest: third-party shareholders in the subsidiary. NCI working for the consolidated SOFP: NCI at acquisition (goodwill working) plus NCI share of post-acquisition reserves.
notes.MID: Mid-year acquisitions: estimate pre-acquisition retained earnings (if not given) — brought-forward retained earnings plus profit for the year pro-rated up to the acquisition date.
notes.FV1: Assets and liabilities in an entity's own financial statements are often not stated at their fair value. The net assets acquired are therefore required to be brought into the consolidated financial statements at their fair value rather than book value.
notes.ORES: Other reserves: pre-acquisition reserves are included in net assets at the date of acquisition (and included in the goodwill calculation). Reserves created post-acquisition, or where there is movement on a reserve existing at acquisition: show in the parent's reserves plus its share of the movement on the subsidiary's reserve.
notes.ICT: Inter-company trading — treat the group as if it were a single entity. Eliminate intragroup revenue and cost of sales: Dr Revenue, Cr Cost of sales for all intragroup trading in the year. Eliminate unrealised profit on goods still in inventory at the year end: Dr Cost of sales, Cr Inventories. Eliminate inter-company balances at the year end: Dr Inter-company payable, Cr Inter-company receivable.

ch25.title: Ch 25 — Consolidated Statement of Profit or Loss

notes.PUR: Show the results of the group as a single business entity.
notes.IGT: Cancel inter-company revenue and cost of sales (for all inter-company sales in the year). Cancel unrealised profit on inventories from inter-company trading left at the year end by increasing the seller's cost of sales — if the subsidiary is the seller, adjust the NCI.
notes.MID: Pro-rate the subsidiary's income, expenses and NCI for the number of months controlled by the parent.

notes.PUR: To provide users with information about financial performance and position and to enable them to make decisions.
notes.ANA: Make a note of all obvious changes or trends before calculating any ratios; give reasons for change and significance for the future.
notes.PROF: Gross profit margin = gross profit / revenue × 100%. Operating profit margin = profit before financing and income taxes / revenue × 100%. Return on capital employed = profit before financing and income taxes / (total equity + non-current liabilities) × 100%. Return on equity = profit for the year less preference dividends / total equity × 100%.
notes.LIQ: Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities (X:1). Quick ratio or acid ratio = (current assets − inventories) / current liabilities (X:1).
notes.EFF: Inventory turnover period = inventories / cost of sales × 365 days. Receivables collection period = trade receivables / revenue × 365 days. Payables payment period = trade payables / cost of sales × 365 days. Working capital cycle = inventory days + receivable days − payable days. Asset turnover = revenue / (total assets − current liabilities) (X times).
notes.POS: Interest cover = profit before financing and income taxes / interest expenses (X times). Gearing = non-current liabilities / (total equity + non-current liabilities) (X times).
notes.LIM: Limitations of ratio analysis: inflation, different accounting policies, lack of information, seasonal trading, year-end figures not representative, related party transactions, different ratio definitions, financial statements manipulated, new company with no comparatives.
